planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to fall in moist but well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this old garden hybrid is far more tolerant of damp ground and partial shade than typical bearded iris.

directions: Holden Clough is a hybrid of uncertain parentage that arose at Holden Clough Nursery in Lancashire, England, and has been grown in cottage gardens for decades on the strength of its unusual coloring and adaptability. Each bloom opens a soft creamy buff-yellow heavily brushed and veined with maroon-brown over the falls, a pattern unlike the self colors or simple bitones typical of bearded iris. It holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliability in borders, woodland edges, and pond-adjacent plantings where ordinary bearded iris would rot. Established clumps are long-lived and resent frequent disturbance, so divide only when flowering noticeably declines.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; this species iris wants steady moisture through the growing season rather than the dry dormancy bearded iris prefer.

directions: Native to damp meadows of Yunnan and Sichuan, Iris chrysographes takes its name from the fine gold veining etched across the falls, and the selection known as 'Black Form' carries that veining over blooms so deeply saturated with velvety purple that they read as nearly black at a distance. Narrow, grass-like foliage forms a tidy clump that stays attractive well after the early-summer bloom passes. It holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and performs best in a rain garden, bog edge, or any border that stays reliably moist through summer. Avoid letting the soil dry out for extended periods, since this species is far less drought-tolerant than bearded iris.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 in deep in well-drained soil in fall; in zones 5-6 apply a winter mulch, and in hot, humid summer climates treat as an annual or lift and store bulbs dry after foliage dies back.

directions: Blue Magic is one of the most widely grown Dutch iris bulb cultivars, opening medium violet-blue standards and falls marked with a bright yellow blaze at the throat on slender, upright stems in late spring. The clean, saturated color and long, straight stems make it a mainstay of the cut-flower trade, with a vase life of roughly a week. After bloom, let the foliage yellow and die back fully before cutting it away, and avoid summer irrigation where the bulbs remain in the ground, since wet dormant soil invites rot.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 in deep in well-drained soil in fall; in zones 5-6 apply a winter mulch, and in hot, humid summer climates treat as an annual or lift and store bulbs dry after foliage dies back.

directions: Purple Sensation is a deeper-toned companion to the more common blue Dutch iris cultivars, opening rich violet-purple standards and falls with a narrow gold streak at the throat on wiry, upright stems in late spring. Its saturated color reads almost black-purple in low light and pairs well with silver or chartreuse foliage companions in a mixed border. Allow the strap-like foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and in regions with wet or humid summers, lift and store the bulbs dry rather than leaving them in the ground, since they are prone to rot in soggy soil.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 in deep in well-drained soil in fall; in zones 5-6 apply a winter mulch, and in hot, humid summer climates treat as an annual or lift and store bulbs dry after foliage dies back.

directions: Telstar is a bicolor Dutch iris cultivar, opening crisp white standards over falls that shade from white at the base into deep blue-violet toward the tip, giving each flower a crisp, two-tone look on slender stems in late spring. The contrast holds up well as a cut flower and stands out in mixed bulb plantings alongside solid-colored Dutch iris cultivars. Let foliage die back naturally before removing it, and lift bulbs for dry summer storage in climates where summer rainfall is heavy, since standing moisture during dormancy causes rot.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 in deep in well-drained soil in fall; in zones 5-6 apply a winter mulch, and in hot, humid summer climates treat as an annual or lift and store bulbs dry after foliage dies back.

directions: Yellow Queen is one of the oldest and most enduring Dutch iris cultivars still widely sold, producing a rich, even golden-yellow self on tall, slender stems in late spring. Its clear, uncomplicated color makes it an easy mixer with blue- and purple-toned Dutch iris cultivars in bulb displays and cutting gardens alike. Allow the grassy foliage to yellow and wither fully before clearing it away, and avoid summer watering over the dormant bulbs, since excess moisture during their rest period leads quickly to rot.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed.

directions: One of the oldest named reticulata iris cultivars still in commerce, 'J.S. Dijt' opens deep reddish-purple flowers with a narrow orange ridge on the falls, carrying a light, sweet fragrance that is easy to miss outdoors but noticeable when picked and brought inside. It flowers low to the ground among slender foliage in very early spring, often alongside snowdrops and crocuses. Like other reticulata cultivars its small bulbs are intolerant of summer moisture, so pair it with other dry-dormancy rock garden plants rather than irrigated border perennials. Allow foliage to die back fully before tidying the planting.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed.

directions: Clairette carries a two-tone blue pattern, with pale sky-blue standards set above deeper violet-blue falls marked by a white streak and dark veining near the orange ridge, opening low among grassy foliage in very early spring. The bicolor effect sets it apart from the more uniformly colored reticulata cultivars already common in gardens, and it naturalizes well in a rock garden or raised bed given sharp drainage. As with all reticulata iris, let the foliage fade and wither on its own after bloom and keep the planting dry through summer dormancy to protect the small bulbs from rot.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed.

directions: Raised in England and long valued as one of the paler reticulata cultivars, Cantab opens soft Cambridge-blue flowers with a deeper blue-violet flush on the falls and a small orange ridge, a gentler color than the more common saturated royal-blue reticulata cultivars. It holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and blooms very early, often pushing up through late snow alongside snowdrops. Give it the same gritty, sharply drained rock garden conditions as other reticulata iris, and avoid summer watering, which rots the small bulbs during their required dry dormancy.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter; spuria iris resent disturbance and should be left undivided for several years once established.

directions: Wadi Zem Zem bears a warm, coppery golden-tan self with a faint bronze sheen across both standards and falls, a muted earth tone that set it apart from the blue, white, and yellow spuria cultivars common when it was introduced by hybridizer Walker Ferguson. Tall, well-branched stems carry the midseason flowers well above narrow, upright foliage, and the cultivar was honored by the Spuria Iris Society for its distinctive color. Water generously from fall regrowth through spring bloom, then allow the soil to dry through summer dormancy, and leave established clumps undisturbed for several years since spurias resent frequent division.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallow, tops exposed, in late summer to fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like the species, this striped-leaf form is grown chiefly as a foliage accent.

directions: Where the already-common gold-striped 'Variegata' form carries creamy yellow stripes, 'Argentea Variegata' instead marks each sword-shaped leaf with crisp white to pale silver longitudinal stripes, giving the clump a cooler, frostier look through the growing season. Fragrant soft blue-lavender flowers, scented of grape or orange blossom, open on tall stems in late spring above the striped fans. Culture matches the species exactly: shallow planting, lean soil, and sharp drainage keep both the stripe pattern crisp and the rhizomes free of rot. It makes an effective companion to the gold-striped form where a gardener wants to pair warm and cool variegated foliage in the same bed.
